title: Methods and Sorting
summary: You will learn how Java methods (Methoden) use parameters (Parameter), return values (Rückgaben), and arrays. Insertion Sort builds a sorted prefix (sortiertes Präfix) by inserting each new element. Reference copying (Referenzkopien), condition order (Reihenfolge der Bedingungen), stability (Stabilität), and quadratic costs are important.
keyFacts: A method is a named, reusable block of code that packages tasks and breaks problems down.
A formal parameter (formaler Parameter) appears in a method definition; an actual argument (aktuelles Argument) is the specific value supplied when the method is called.
A void method returns no value and is also called a procedure (Prozedur).
A precondition (Vorbedingung) must hold before a call; min requires a nonempty array because it reads b[0].
The words after the class name are passed as strings in main(String[] args).
In an assignment such as int result = min(a), result is initialized only after min returns.
Java copies each argument value when a method is called: for a primitive type it copies the value, and for an array it copies the reference.
A method can change the shared array with b[0] = 9; by contrast, b = new int[2] only reassigns the local reference.
Two variables that point to the same array exhibit aliasing; a true copy requires a new array and copying its elements.
Insertion Sort builds a sorted prefix step by step and returns a sorted copy of the input.
locate determines the insertion position; shift copies the affected elements to the right, after which x is written at position j.
shift runs from right to left so that values are not overwritten before they are copied.
In j < i && x >= b[j], if the left side is false, the right side is not evaluated; this prevents b[i] from being read.
With x >= b[j], locate moves past equal elements, so the new element is placed after them and the sort remains stable.
In iteration i, locate and shift together take about i steps; in total, 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 ∈ Θ(n²).
After inserting a[i], b[0..i] is sorted and contains exactly the first i + 1 input values.

review.notes: Geprüft: 44 Fragen. Ergänzt wurde beim Boss-Sortierbeispiel der fehlende Algorithmus im Kontext, damit die Instanz ohne Vorlesung lösbar ist. Antworten, Distraktoren, Erklärungen, Mermaid-Diagramme und verify-Skripte geprüft.

questions.prompt: What is a method in Java?

options.text: A variable that exists only in main
An expression that always returns a value
An array with a fixed length
A named, reusable block of code

questions.explanation: A method groups statements under a name. It can be reused and helps break a problem into smaller tasks.

questions.prompt: In `public static int min(int[] b)`, `b` is a ___.

options.text: Return value
Command-line argument
Actual argument
Formal parameter

questions.explanation: A formal parameter is the input variable in a method definition. An actual argument is the specific value supplied when the method is called, such as `a` in `min(a)`.

questions.prompt: A `return` statement ends the current method call and can return a value.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: `return result;` ends the call and returns `result` to the calling location.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe benefits of methods? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: A problem can be broken down into smaller tasks.
Every method must return an array.
A code block written once can be called repeatedly.
Several steps are given a name.

questions.explanation: Methods package tasks, allow reuse, and support breaking a problem down. A return type can also be `void`.

questions.prompt: What is a method with return type `void` also called?

options.text: Invariant
Procedure
Constructor
Actual argument

questions.explanation: A `void` method returns no value and is also called a procedure.

options.text: Hel lo World!
HelloWorld!
World!loHel
TestHelloWorld!

questions.explanation: `args[0]`, `args[1]`, and `args[2]` are the strings `Hel`, `lo`, and `World!`. Concatenation joins them without adding spaces.

questions.prompt: In the diagram, `main` waits while `min(a)` is executed. What does the return arrow from `min` mean?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  M["main: int result = min(a)"] -. "call" .-> F["min: check values"]
  F --> R["return result"]
  R -. "return" .-> W["main: assign result, then write"]
context.caption: Call and return between main and min

options.text: `min` is started again without arguments.
The local variable in `min` becomes the local variable in `main`.
Execution jumps back to the beginning of the program.
The return value goes back to the waiting call in `main`.

questions.explanation: After `return result`, execution returns to the waiting method call. There, `main` can use the return value.

questions.prompt: The method `min(int[] b)` begins with `int result = b[0];`. What precondition does it need for this access to be valid?

options.text: The array must contain exactly two elements.
All elements must be positive.
The array must already be sorted.
The array must contain at least one element.

questions.explanation: An empty array has no element at index 0. Therefore, the array must be nonempty for this access.

questions.prompt: A local variable named `result` in `main` and a local variable named `result` in `min` are the same variable.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Local variables are valid only within their respective blocks. Using the same name in two methods does not make them the same variable.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `main(String[] args)` are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `args[0]` always contains the class name.
Words after the class name are stored as strings in `args`.
`main` is the program's entry point.
`args` contains only numbers.

questions.explanation: `main` is the program's entry point. The words given after the class name when the program starts are stored as strings in `args`.

questions.prompt: In the method header `public static int[] readArray(int number)`, `int[]` is the ___.

options.text: Return type
Body
Method name
Formal parameters

questions.explanation: The return type specifies the type of value the method returns. Here, it is an array of `int` values.

options.text: The call causes an error.
There is no output.

questions.explanation: `zero` receives a copy of the `int` value. The assignment `number = 0` changes this local copy, while `n` retains the value 2.

questions.explanation: The argument's value is a reference to the same array. `b[0] = 9` mutates this shared array, so `a[0]` reads 9 afterward.

questions.prompt: Given `int[] a = {4, 8}; min(a);`, what is the actual argument in the call `min(a)`?

options.text: The specific value to which `a` refers
The formal parameter `b`
The method body of `min`
The return type `int`

questions.explanation: The actual argument is the specific value supplied when the method is called. Here, it is the array reference stored in `a`.

questions.prompt: For `locate(b, x, i)`, `j` starts at 0 and is incremented while `j < i && x >= b[j]` is true. Given `b = [1, 4, 8, 10]`, `x = 6`, and `i = 4`, which index does `locate` return?
questions.explanation: `6 >= 1` and `6 >= 4` are true, so `j` reaches 2. At that point `6 >= 8` is false, so 2 is returned.

questions.prompt: For `shift(b, j, i)`, `b[k + 1] = b[k]` is executed while `k` runs downward from `i - 1` to `j`. How many assignments occur for `j = 2` and `i = 5`?
questions.explanation: `k` takes the values 4, 3, and 2. Thus, the assignment is executed exactly three times.

questions.prompt: In the process, `j < i` holds, but `x >= b[j]` is false. Which step is executed next?

context.caption: Find the position, shift elements, and insert the value

options.text: `return j`

questions.explanation: The loop condition is false overall because the comparison with `b[j]` fails. The process exits `locate` and then begins shifting with `k = i - 1`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `int[] b = a` are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `a` and `b` then refer to the same array.
The assignment copies all array elements into a new array.
A change to `b[0]` is also visible through `a[0]`.
`a` is automatically redirected to a new array.

questions.explanation: The assignment copies the reference, not the array. Therefore, both variables point to the same elements.

questions.prompt: In `insert`, the steps are executed in this order: `locate`, `shift`, then `___`.

options.text: `b = new int[i]`
`return b[j]`

questions.explanation: First, the insertion position is determined; then elements are shifted to the right. Finally, `x` is placed at the freed position `j`.

questions.prompt: If `copy(a)` creates and returns a new array with the same elements, later changes to this new array are not automatically changes to `a`.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A true copy is a separate array. Unlike a simple reference assignment, the two variables do not share the same array.

questions.prompt: When sorting the input `{8, 3, 6}`, after inserting the first element into the result array `b`, what is the sorted prefix?

options.text: The prefix is empty until all values have been inserted.

questions.explanation: After the first iteration, only `a[0]`, that is, 8, has been inserted. A single element already forms a sorted prefix.

questions.prompt: Why does the index check come first in `while (j < i && x >= b[j])`? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Swapping the order would be equally safe for every possible array and every `i`.
If `j < i` is false, `b[j]` is not read because of short-circuit evaluation.
The order ensures that `b[j]` always takes the value `x`.
This skips the right side of the condition when `j = i`.

questions.explanation: With `&&`, the right side is checked only if the left side is true. If `j = i`, `j < i` therefore prevents an access to `b[j]`.

questions.prompt: In `locate` with condition `x >= b[j]`, `j` moves past equal values. As a result, a new element of equal value is inserted after them.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The comparison `>=` allows the search to continue even when values are equal. The new element is placed after the existing equal values, preserving their order.

questions.prompt: When shifting `[1, 3, 7, 9, 0]` to make an insertion starting at `j = 2`, why does `shift` run from right to left?

options.text: So that each value is copied before its position is overwritten.
So that the array gets a new length.
So that `j` grows automatically during the shift.
So that the values in the result are sorted in descending order.

questions.explanation: Working from right to left preserves every value that still needs to be copied. If elements were shifted from left to right, for example, the 9 would be overwritten before it was copied.

source.heading: Warum von rechts nach links schieben?

questions.prompt: An array with $n=6$ values is built using the described variant of Insertion Sort. The insertions take place at indices $i=1,2,3,4,5$. In this cost model, inserting at index $i$ takes exactly $i$ steps. How many steps are needed in total?
questions.explanation: The insertions take $1+2+3+4+5=15$ steps.
First, 4 is inserted; then 1 is placed before it; finally, 3 is inserted between 1 and 4. The result array therefore contains 1, 3, 4.

questions.prompt: What does the invariant assert after inserting `a[i]`?

options.text: `b` is already completely sorted after every iteration.
`b[i..n-1]` is sorted and contains all input values.
`b[0..i]` is sorted and contains exactly the first `i + 1` input values.
`b[0..i]` contains only values greater than `a[i]`.

questions.explanation: After each iteration, the initial portion through index `i` forms a sorted prefix. It contains exactly the input values processed up to and including `a[i]`.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the process after each iteration?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["Before iteration i: b[0..i-1] is sorted"] --> B["Insert a[i] in the right place"]
  B --> C["Afterward: b[0..i] is sorted"]
  C --> D{"i = n - 1?"}
  D -- "no" --> A
  D -- "yes" --> E["b is a sorted copy of a"]
context.caption: The invariant across iterations

options.text: Before the first iteration, the entire result array is sorted and filled.
At `i = n - 1`, `b` contains only the last input element.
After the iteration for `i`, `b[0..i]` is sorted.
The algorithm sorts the input by directly modifying `a`.

questions.explanation: Each step inserts `a[i]` into the sorted prefix built so far. Therefore, after the final insertion, the entire array `b` is sorted.

questions.prompt: Suppose `b` has length 3 and a modified loop condition is `x >= b[j] && j < i`. When `j = i = 3` is reached, which access is attempted first?

options.text: `b[3]` is read first; this index is outside an array of length 3.
`j < i` is checked first, and the array access is skipped.
The condition is treated as true without evaluating either part.
The value `x` is written to `b[3]`.

questions.explanation: With `&&`, the expression is evaluated from left to right. With the order reversed, `x >= b[j]` is evaluated first; at `j = 3`, this accesses the invalid index 3.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the cost of iteration `i` are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Together, they always take `i²` steps.
The input determines whether `j` cancels out in the sum.
`locate` takes about `j` steps and `shift` takes exactly `i - j` steps.
Together, they take about `i` steps, independent of `j`.

questions.explanation: The subtasks add up to `j + (i - j) = i`. The value of `j` cancels out, so this estimate does not depend on the input.

questions.prompt: This variant takes Θ(n²) even on an already sorted input because `locate` searches from the left through the prefix in every iteration.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Even for sorted input, `locate` runs from index 0 to nearly `i`. The sum of these search lengths grows quadratically.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture notes, what does inlining a method call mean?

options.text: The JVM can automatically replace the call with the method body.
The method is always converted into an array.
The compiler deletes all local variables.
The caller terminates after the call.

questions.explanation: Inlining means replacing a call with the method body. The JVM can perform this transformation automatically.

questions.prompt: A route-planning program considers routes in the order A, B, C. A takes 7 minutes and has no stairs; B takes 5 minutes and has no stairs; C also takes 5 minutes and has no stairs. The rule selects the fastest route without stairs; in a tie, the route selected first remains selected. Which route is selected?

options.text: No suitable route
B, because it is the first fastest route
A, because it comes first
C, because a tie favors the later route

questions.explanation: A is selected first, then replaced by the faster route B. C is not faster than B, so B remains selected in the tie.
`b = a` copies the reference, so both variables point to the same array. The change through `b[1]` is visible when reading through `a[1]`.

options.text: Accessing `b[0]` throws an exception.
There is no output.
false
true

questions.explanation: `b.length` is 0, so `j < b.length` is false. Because of short-circuit evaluation, `b[j]` is not read, and `safe` remains `false`.
`x[0] = y` first changes the shared array. `y = 100` changes only the local copy; after `x` is reassigned, `x[1] = 50` affects only the new array.

questions.prompt: The approximate step count for this sorting variant is $T(n)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. How many steps are needed for $n=1000$?
questions.explanation: $1000\cdot999/2=499\,500$. The leading quadratic term explains the Θ(n²) growth.

questions.prompt: Which statements about sorting with helper methods are correct? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `insert` changes array `b` even though it returns no value.
`sort` creates `b` and calls `insert` for each input element.
`locate` shifts the elements to the right.
`shift` determines the insertion position.

questions.explanation: `sort` creates the result array and inserts the values one at a time. `insert` mutates the shared array; `locate` finds the position, while `shift` shifts the elements.

questions.prompt: What result follows from the final path in the diagram if processing continues through `i = n - 1`?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["Before iteration i: b[0..i-1] is sorted"] --> B["Insert a[i] in the right place"]
  B --> C["Afterward: b[0..i] is sorted"]
  C --> D{"i = n - 1?"}
  D -- "no" --> A
  D -- "yes" --> E["b is a sorted copy of a"]
context.caption: From the sorted prefix to the complete result

options.text: `b` contains only a sorted prefix, with no remaining values.
`a` has been completely overwritten and contains only the last element.
`b` is a sorted copy of `a`.
`b` contains the values in reverse order.

questions.explanation: After each insertion, the prefix through `i` is sorted. When `i` reaches the last index, this prefix covers the entire result array and contains all the input values.

questions.prompt: Run Insertion Sort using `locate` and `shift` on `a = [17, 3, -2, 9, 0, 1, 7, 42, 5]`. Which values does the returned array contain in ascending order?

context.caption: Algorithm for inserting into a sorted prefix

questions.explanation: Each element is inserted into the sorted prefix. All nine input values are preserved, giving `-2, 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 17, 42` in ascending order.

questions.prompt: Consider `int result = min(a); write(result);`. `min` computes its own local `result` internally and returns it with `return result`. When is the local value assigned in `main`?

options.text: Only after `min` has returned.
During each loop iteration of `min`, directly in `main`.
It is never assigned because `min` has a local variable.
Before `min` is called.

questions.explanation: While `min` runs, `main` waits at the call site. Only after that does the return value initialize `result` in `main`; the two local variables are distinct.

questions.prompt: A method receives `int[] x` and `int y`. It executes `x[0] = y; y = 100; x = new int[1];`. The caller had `a = {7}` and `v = 3`. What is true after the call? More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `a` now points to the method's new array.
`v` is 3.

questions.explanation: `x[0] = y` changes the shared array using the copied value 3. The change to `y` affects only the local copy, and reassigning `x` does not change `a`.

questions.prompt: `insert` can change the result array without returning a value because the copied parameter `b` still points to the same array as the one in the caller.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A return value is not needed for this: `b` contains a copy of the reference and lets the method change the shared array elements.

levels.title: Practice: Sorting Tricks in Everyday Life

questions.prompt: Three views in a campus app need to use the same sequence of steps to display a place name consistently. Which solution makes good use of methods?

options.text: Create a separate copy of the entire place-data array in each view.
Pass the place name to the app as a command-line argument.
Sort the views by place name to make the code reusable.
Group the steps in a named method once and call it from all three views.

questions.explanation: A method groups a task under a name and can be reused in several places. This helps keep the views consistent.

questions.prompt: You start a Java tool in a terminal and want to pass it a file name and an option. Where do the words after the class name go in `main(String[] args)`?

options.text: As elements of the array `args`.
As the return value of `main`.
As local variables in every called method.
As elements of an automatically sorted array.

questions.explanation: Java passes the words after the class name as strings in the array `args`. The tool can interpret them as, for example, a file name and an option.

questions.prompt: Use this cost model for Insertion Sort: For `n` values, the work for `locate` and `shift` together takes `1 + 2 + … + (n − 1)` steps. How many steps are needed for 40 values?
questions.explanation: The sum is $1 + 2 + \dots + 39 = \frac{40 \cdot 39}{2} = 780$ steps.

questions.prompt: A Java app stores seats in a `boolean[]`. A method receives this array and sets `b[4] = true`; the array has at least five elements. What does the calling app see after the method call?

options.text: The method automatically works on a complete copy of the array.
The app's reference is set to a new array.
Its array also has the value `true` at index 4.
Only the local variable `b` changes; the app's array remains unchanged.

questions.explanation: The array reference is copied during the call, so both variables still point to the same array. Therefore, a change to an element is also visible to the app.

questions.prompt: A transit app initially displays connections in input order, then sorts them by departure minute. A stable sort keeps entries with the same sort key in their original order. What happens to two connections with the same departure minute?

options.text: They are always ordered alphabetically by destination.
The connection appearing later in the input always comes first.
One of the two connections is removed.
Their original order is preserved.

questions.explanation: Stability preserves the order of entries with equal sort keys. Thus, connections with the same departure minute retain their previous order.

questions.prompt: Under the same cost model, the work for `n` values is `1 + 2 + … + (n − 1)`. By what factor does the work increase from 20 to 40 values, rounded to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: For 20 values, the work takes $190$ steps; for 40 values, it takes $780$. The ratio is $780 / 190 \approx 4{,}1$.

questions.prompt: A dashboard keeps a list of sales sorted in ascending order by amount. For each new sale, it finds the right place in the already sorted list and shifts the following entries to the right. Which algorithm illustrates this process?

options.text: Short-circuit evaluation: a second condition is sometimes skipped.
Insertion Sort: insert new values step by step in the appropriate position.
Aliasing: several variables point to the same array.
Call and Return: a method returns its result.

questions.explanation: Insertion Sort keeps a prefix sorted and inserts each new value in the appropriate position. The following entries are shifted to the right to make room.

questions.prompt: A gallery app creates a new `int[]` for 64 ratings. A loop copies each element exactly once into the new array. How many element assignments does the loop perform?
questions.explanation: There is exactly one assignment to the new array copy for each of the 64 elements. That makes 64 assignments in total.

questions.prompt: In Java, you check whether a measurement exists at position `pos` and is nonnegative. With `&&`, the right side is evaluated only if the left side is true. Which condition checks the bounds before reading `samples[pos]`?

options.text: `pos < samples.length && samples[pos] >= 0`
`samples[pos] >= 0 && pos >= 0 && pos < samples.length`
`pos >= 0 && pos < samples.length && samples[pos] >= 0`
`samples[pos] >= 0`

questions.explanation: First, the check verifies that `pos` is nonnegative and less than the array length. Because of short-circuit evaluation, `samples[pos]` is read only if both bounds checks are true.

questions.prompt: An app calculates the total price using `int total = priceFor(cart);` and then displays it. What must happen before `total` contains the return value?

options.text: The app must first sort `cart` to make a return value possible.
`priceFor` must directly change the local variable `total`.
`total` is automatically set to the final price before the call.
`priceFor` is called, calculates the value, and returns with `return`.

questions.explanation: The synchronous call returns only after `priceFor` has calculated and returned the value. The returned value is then assigned to `total` and can be displayed.
